div.head: CHn cor 2
div.ab: Si quis baronum meorum, comitum siue aliorum qui de me tenent, mortuus fuerit, heres suus non redimet terram suam, sicut faciebat tempore fratris mei, sed legitima et iusta releuatione releuabit eam.
Si quis baronum meorum, comitum sive aliorum qui de me tenent, mortuus fuerit, heres suus non redimet terram suam sicut faciebat tempore fratris mei, sed iusta et legitima relevatione relevabit eam.
If any of my barons, earls or other tenants-in-chief has died, his heir shall not redeem his land as he did in the time of my brother, but he shall pay the just and lawful relief for it.
div.note: Added October 2026 from Robertson pp. 276–277 (text and translation); Liebermann’s text added from Gesetze I p. 521, October 2026 (two independent readings of the page images)

Ich glaube nicht (mit Price Anc. laws p. 267), hier sei die an Einzelheiten reiche Verfügung über Mutung in Leis Wl 20ff. gemeint, vielmehr wohl nur die 5 £ fürs Ritterlehn (Dial. de Scacc. II 10 ed. Hughes p. 223). Eine feste Summe ist aber gemeint; sonst hätte c. 2 keinen Vorteil für den Vassallen und 2, 1 für den Aftervassallen bedeutet. Freilich blieb tatsächlich im 12. Jh. die Mutung der Kronlehnsträger in der Willkür des Königs: dies könnte, wie beim Regalienrecht, auf Versprechensbruch des Königs beruhen. Die Wilhelm dem II. geschuldeten Mutungen des rechten Lehnserben erlässt u. 6, 1, wo noch einmal deutlich wird, dass dieser sie willkürlich vereinbart hatte. Den Satz benutzt ‘Unknown ch. (o. Einl. 13)’ 2

I do not believe (with Price Anc. laws p. 267) that the provision on relief in Leis Wl 20ff., rich in detail, is meant here; rather, probably, only the 5 £ for a knight’s fee (Dial. de Scacc. II 10 ed. Hughes p. 223). A fixed sum, however, is meant; otherwise c. 2 would have meant no advantage for the vassal, nor 2, 1 for the sub-vassal. Admittedly, in the 12th cent. the relief of tenants-in-chief in practice remained at the king’s discretion: this could, as with the regalian right, rest on the king’s breach of his promise. The reliefs owed to William II by the rightful heir to a fief are remitted below 6, 1, where it becomes clear once again that he had fixed them arbitrarily. The sentence is used by ‘Unknown ch. (above Introduction 13)’ 2
